record.tranche_reason: Tests whether SAE reconstruction errors have unusually large effects on model predictions using activation substitutions and output-distribution measures; it does not measure the linear predictability or scaling properties in the claim.
record.gate_note: The post reports outcome comparisons for SAE substitutions and random perturbation controls. It also refers to plots for detailed layerwise distributions, position breakdowns, and token examples; numerical values not stated in the text are not inferred.
record.test_reason: The post directly measures whether SAE-reconstruction substitution harms GPT2-small's next-token KL and loss more than random substitutions at equal L2 error. This is the comparison V3 names and the one the original paper reuses, so T1 rather than T2. The post is not the listed original source. Its SAE-norm control also bears on whether uniform norm shrinkage explains the effect (V6).
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The author concludes that SAE reconstructions make systematic, non-random errors. Residual-stream substitution raises KL and loss about 2–4.5x over equal-L2 random substitution, and this is not caused by norm shrinkage. KL gaps should become a standard SAE faithfulness metric. The cause is unknown; the author's hypotheses include a non-isotropic baseline, dense features under L1, nonlinear features, undertraining, the training recipe, and a quirk of GPT2. The author also asks for replication.
record.recipe_differences: Uses SAE activation substitutions and random perturbations matched by L2 error, cosine similarity, or norm, then measures model-output KL and loss. The study does not measure linear predictability of the error.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported effect varies with SAE type (residual stream versus attention), layer, whether all tokens or one token are substituted, and the perturbation/norm-matching method.

fits_no_version.finding: The per-token KL gap correlates most strongly with the KL gap at other layers. Some tokens are consistently hard for SAEs, with no correlation to token frequency. The gap also varies with position and weakly with L0.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE pathological-error tokens are consistent across layers (cross-layer analogue of V2's same-context failures).

record.problems: The main results are on GPT2-small; the author notes that broader replication is needed. The post itself notes that the ε-random baseline may be inappropriate if activation space is non-isotropic. Detailed layerwise plots and some numerical distributions are not present in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed per-layer histogram values, the 99.9th-percentile values, position breakdowns, and individual token-example values are referenced in plots but are not stated numerically in the text; they were not separately extracted.

untested.parts: Linear predictability of the SAE error from the input activation is not measured.
Error norms across SAE sizes, and persistence with scale, are not measured. Only one 32x SAE per layer is used.
The error is not split into linear and nonlinear parts. Whether either part resists dictionary learning is not measured.
No circuit or steering analysis with or without the error term.

Untested: whether dark matter shrinks with other architectures, end-to-end training, more training FLOPs, or a different L1/L0 recipe, and the role of dead latents. The author lists these only as hypotheses. Non-uniform feature suppression, as with scale fine-tuning, is not tested.

missing.what: For attention SAEs, a larger fraction of the SAE-vs-random gap is due to norm change, depending on layer.
In single-token intervention the KL gap persists through the following 16 tokens, with magnitude depending on layer depth.
The whole KL distribution is shifted (not driven by outliers), per layer histograms with 99.9th percentiles.
missing.locator: Layerwise Intervention Results in More Detail

missing.what: Cross-layer correlation of the per-token KL gap; relation to cosine similarity, L0 and position.

record.verdict_notes: Results are GPT2-small only, using Bloom residual SAEs and Kissane et al. attention SAEs. The author and commenters (Nanda) flag that the ε-random baseline may be unfair if activation space is anisotropic. That caveat is an untested hypothesis, not a result. A commenter (Riggs) reports a different result for GPT2 attn_out layer 0 with cosine-matched perturbations. The V6 verdict is narrow: it covers uniform norm rescaling only, not feature-wise suppression.

versions.untested_parts: Whether a large share of SAE error is linearly predictable from the input activation.
Whether per-token error norms are predictable across SAE sizes, larger SAEs fail on the same contexts, or error persists with scale.
The post measures KL divergence and cross-entropy loss after substitutions, but does not test other measures of how the error affects model computation.
Whether linearly predictable error contains unlearned features and whether nonlinear error resists dictionary learning.
Whether feature-based circuits or steering analyses lose behavior when the error term is omitted.

It tests whether the norm change alone explains the effect, but does not test dead latents, alternative objectives, improved architectures, end-to-end training, or whether dark matter generally shrinks under those changes.
